questions.unit_title: Chapter 7: On the Topic of Imam al-Hassan al-‘Askari
questions.prompt: Why does Mutahhari describe Imam al-Hasan al-‘Askari as an Imam who lived under extreme pressure?
questions.answer: Mutahhari explains that the closer the line of Imams came to the era of the Imam of the Time, the more difficult their task became. Imam al-‘Askari lived at a time when belief in the promised Mahdi was widespread and people expected the Mahdi to emerge from his line. The authorities therefore treated the Imam and his household as a serious object of surveillance. His circumstances were not simply those of a religious leader facing ordinary political opposition; the regime was particularly anxious about the birth and succession associated with him.
questions.source_locator: Chapter 7: On the Topic of Imam al-Hassan al-‘Askari

questions.unit_title: Chapter 7: On the Topic of Imam al-Hassan al-‘Askari
questions.prompt: Why was the centre of government transferred from Baghdad to Samarra during the time of al-Mu‘tasim, according to Mutahhari?
questions.answer: Mutahhari says that the transfer followed complaints about the oppressive conduct of al-Mu‘tasim’s army toward the people of Baghdad. The people complained, and although al-Mu‘tasim did not agree at first, he eventually accepted the transfer of the government centre to Samarra so that the army would be farther from the population. The explanation provides the political background for the Imam’s later residence in Samarra. It also shows that the move was connected with the army’s relationship with the people, not originally described simply as a measure against the Imam.
questions.source_locator: Chapter 7: On the Topic of Imam al-Hassan al-‘Askari

questions.unit_title: Chapter 7: On the Topic of Imam al-Hassan al-‘Askari
questions.prompt: What was al-‘Askar or al-‘Askari, and why was Imam al-‘Askari compelled to live there?
questions.answer: Mutahhari explains that Imam al-‘Askari and Imam al-Hadi were compelled to reside in an area of Samarra called al-‘Askar or al-‘Askari, a name associated with the army and its base. Their residence was deliberately situated within a military environment so that the authorities could keep them under close surveillance. The location therefore functioned as an instrument of political control: it made it easier to monitor the Imams, restrict their visitors, and limit their contact with followers. The chapter emphasizes that the Imam’s confinement was built into the place where he was forced to live.
questions.source_locator: Chapter 7: On the Topic of Imam al-Hassan al-‘Askari

questions.unit_title: Chapter 7: On the Topic of Imam al-Hassan al-‘Askari
questions.prompt: What were Imam al-‘Askari’s age at death, the approximate age of his father at death, and the duration of his Imamate?
questions.answer: According to the figures given by Mutahhari, Imam al-‘Askari died at the age of twenty-eight. His father, Imam al-Hadi, was approximately forty-two when he passed away. Imam al-‘Askari’s own period of Imamate lasted only six years. These details establish the brevity of his public leadership and help explain why the chapter emphasizes the severe restrictions under which he had to guide the community. The six-year period should be stated distinctly from the Imam’s age at death.
questions.source_locator: Chapter 7: On the Topic of Imam al-Hassan al-‘Askari

questions.unit_title: Chapter 7: On the Topic of Imam al-Hassan al-‘Askari
questions.prompt: What restrictions did Imam al-‘Askari face during his six years of Imamate?
questions.answer: Mutahhari says that during the six years of his Imamate, Imam al-‘Askari was either imprisoned or, when not in prison, prevented from ordinary social contact and visits. The restriction affected the normal channels through which an Imam could teach, meet followers, answer questions, and maintain contact with the community. The chapter therefore portrays his leadership as being exercised under confinement and surveillance. The point is not merely that he faced political hostility, but that the authorities attempted to isolate him from the people who sought his guidance.
questions.source_locator: Chapter 7: On the Topic of Imam al-Hassan al-‘Askari

questions.unit_title: Chapter 7: On the Topic of Imam al-Hassan al-‘Askari
questions.prompt: Which quality does Mutahhari identify as especially characteristic of Imam al-‘Askari, and how did it affect even his opponents?
questions.answer: Mutahhari identifies dignity and an impressive bearing as especially characteristic of Imam al-‘Askari. He says that visitors could be affected by the greatness visible in the Imam’s face even before he spoke. The effect was not limited to followers: even enemies and officials who pursued him and sometimes took him to prison could not help showing respect when they encountered him. Mutahhari uses these reports to illustrate the influence of the Imam’s character despite the absence of political freedom or official power.
questions.source_locator: Chapter 7: On the Topic of Imam al-Hassan al-‘Askari

questions.unit_title: Chapter 7: On the Topic of Imam al-Hassan al-‘Askari
questions.prompt: Which report does Mutahhari mention when discussing the dignity of Imam al-‘Askari, and what does he say about it?
questions.answer: Mutahhari refers to a story narrated by Muhaddith Qummi in Al-Anwar al-Bahiyyah. The report is transmitted from Ahmad ibn ‘Ubayd Allah ibn Khaqan, the son of a minister, and concerns an event in which his father was present. Mutahhari describes it as an extraordinary account but says that he does not have time in that lecture to narrate it fully. A careful answer should not invent the missing details. The important point is that Mutahhari appeals to a report associated with a source and a witness connected to the government to illustrate the Imam’s dignity and the respect he commanded.
questions.source_locator: Chapter 7: On the Topic of Imam al-Hassan al-‘Askari

questions.unit_title: Chapter 7: On the Topic of Imam al-Hassan al-‘Askari
questions.prompt: Why did the Abbasid authorities intensify their surveillance of Imam al-‘Askari?
questions.answer: Mutahhari explains that it was widely known that the promised Mahdi would emerge from the line of Imam al-‘Askari. The authorities feared that the birth of this child would threaten their rule, so they closely monitored the Imam’s home and household. Mutahhari compares their actions with Pharaoh’s response to the prediction that a child from Bani Isra’il would bring about his downfall. The comparison explains the author’s interpretation of the regime’s motive: surveillance was directed not only against the Imam himself but also against the possibility of the birth and survival of the promised successor.
questions.source_locator: Chapter 7: On the Topic of Imam al-Hassan al-‘Askari

questions.unit_title: Chapter 7: On the Topic of Imam al-Hassan al-‘Askari
questions.prompt: What is the Pharaoh analogy used by Mutahhari, and which details make the comparison relevant?
questions.answer: Mutahhari recalls the account of Pharaoh, who feared a foretold child from Bani Isra’il and responded by killing newborn boys and appointing women to inspect households and identify pregnancies. He compares this with the Abbasid authorities’ surveillance of Imam al-‘Askari’s household because they feared the birth of the promised Mahdi from the Imam’s line. In both accounts, political power attempts to prevent a feared future by monitoring births and targeting a vulnerable household. The analogy is used to explain the authorities’ fear and methods; it does not mean that every historical detail of the two situations was identical.
questions.source_locator: Chapter 7: On the Topic of Imam al-Hassan al-‘Askari

questions.unit_title: Chapter 7: On the Topic of Imam al-Hassan al-‘Askari
questions.prompt: When were searches of Imam al-‘Askari’s house especially frequent, and what prompted them?
questions.answer: Mutahhari says that officials periodically sent people to search the Imam’s house, especially when Imam al-‘Askari died. The authorities had repeatedly heard reports that Imam al-Mahdi had already been born, so the Imam’s death intensified their efforts to find the child. The searches show that the state was acting on the fear that the promised successor existed and might be concealed in the household. They do not establish that the officials actually found the child or obtained reliable knowledge of his whereabouts.
questions.source_locator: Chapter 7: On the Topic of Imam al-Hassan al-‘Askari

questions.unit_title: Chapter 7: On the Topic of Imam al-Hassan al-‘Askari
questions.prompt: How does Mutahhari describe the concealment of Imam al-Mahdi’s birth and the limited disclosure of his identity?
questions.answer: Mutahhari says that the birth of Imam al-Mahdi was concealed by divine protection and that only a small number of people knew of it at the time. During the child’s early life, Imam al-‘Askari introduced him to special Shi‘ah followers who came from different places, while the general public remained unaware. Eventually, news spread that a son had been born to Imam al-‘Askari and was being hidden. The account therefore distinguishes between the limited group of trusted followers who were informed and the wider public, who did not have direct access to the child.
questions.source_locator: Chapter 7: On the Topic of Imam al-Hassan al-‘Askari

questions.unit_title: Chapter 7: On the Topic of Imam al-Hassan al-‘Askari
questions.prompt: How old was Imam al-Mahdi when Imam al-‘Askari passed away, according to the chapter?
questions.answer: Mutahhari states that Imam al-Mahdi was six years old when his father, Imam al-‘Askari, passed away. This detail is important because the chapter describes the transition to the period of occultation while the promised Imam was still a child. It also helps explain why the community relied on trusted figures who could answer practical questions and preserve continuity while the Imam remained concealed.
questions.source_locator: Chapter 7: On the Topic of Imam al-Hassan al-‘Askari

questions.unit_title: Chapter 7: On the Topic of Imam al-Hassan al-‘Askari
questions.prompt: What happened when the authorities searched the household after Imam al-‘Askari’s death?
questions.answer: After Imam al-‘Askari’s death, officials entered the household and searched it thoroughly. They also sent women to inspect the women of the household, including slave girls, in order to determine whether any of them might be pregnant. The authorities suspected one slave girl and detained her for a year. They eventually realized that the suspicion was mistaken. Mutahhari uses the incident to show how far the surveillance extended: it reached beyond the Imam himself and subjected women in the household to intrusive searches and detention.
questions.source_locator: Chapter 7: On the Topic of Imam al-Hassan al-‘Askari

questions.unit_title: Chapter 7: On the Topic of Imam al-Hassan al-‘Askari
questions.prompt: Who was Hudayth, and why was she known as Jaddah?
questions.answer: Mutahhari identifies Hudayth as the mother of Imam al-‘Askari. She became known by the title Jaddah, meaning “grandmother,” because of her relationship to the Imam of the Time. The title reflected her connection with the hidden Imam, but Mutahhari emphasizes that her reputation did not rest only on being his grandmother. She had her own standing, dignity, learning, and personality, which made her an important figure for the Shi‘ah community after Imam al-‘Askari’s death.
questions.source_locator: Chapter 7: On the Topic of Imam al-Hassan al-‘Askari

questions.unit_title: Chapter 7: On the Topic of Imam al-Hassan al-‘Askari
questions.prompt: Why does Mutahhari insist that Jaddah’s importance was not merely the result of her family relationship?
questions.answer: Mutahhari says that although Hudayth was known as Jaddah because she was the grandmother of the Imam of the Time, kinship alone did not explain her reputation. She possessed personal status, greatness, and a special personality, and these qualities are described in historical accounts. The chapter presents her as a learned and respected woman in her own right. This distinction matters because it prevents her role from being reduced to a family title: she became a source of guidance and refuge because of her own knowledge and standing.
questions.source_locator: Chapter 7: On the Topic of Imam al-Hassan al-‘Askari

questions.unit_title: Chapter 7: On the Topic of Imam al-Hassan al-‘Askari
questions.prompt: What role did Jaddah play for the Shi‘ah community after Imam al-‘Askari’s death?
questions.answer: Mutahhari cites Muhaddith Qummi’s description of Jaddah as the shelter or refuge of the Shi‘ah after Imam al-‘Askari. When followers encountered religious or doctrinal problems, they brought their questions to her. Her learning and personal standing allowed her to help the community at a time when the Imam was concealed and ordinary access to him was not possible. The chapter therefore presents her as an important figure in the continuity of religious guidance, not as a replacement for the Imam’s actual authority.
questions.source_locator: Chapter 7: On the Topic of Imam al-Hassan al-‘Askari

questions.unit_title: Chapter 7: On the Topic of Imam al-Hassan al-‘Askari
questions.prompt: What did Hakimah Khatun say about the identity of the Imam during occultation and whom people should consult for practical questions?
questions.answer: Hakimah Khatun, the daughter of Imam al-Jawad and aunt of Imam al-‘Askari, stated that the hidden child of Imam al-‘Askari was her Imam even though he was in occultation. When asked whom people should consult if they had problems, she directed them to Jaddah. She therefore distinguished the identity of the true Imam from the person who could serve as the visible point of reference for practical questions. The arrangement preserved the belief in the hidden Imam while recognizing the practical role of a trusted and learned woman in the community.
questions.source_locator: Chapter 7: On the Topic of Imam al-Hassan al-‘Askari

questions.unit_title: Chapter 7: On the Topic of Imam al-Hassan al-‘Askari
questions.prompt: Explain how the political geography of Samarra and the military quarter contributed to the surveillance of Imam al-‘Askari.
questions.answer: Mutahhari first explains that the government centre was moved from Baghdad to Samarra during the time of al-Mu‘tasim after complaints about the army’s oppressive behaviour toward the people. Imam al-Hadi and Imam al-‘Askari were then compelled to reside in an area called al-‘Askar or al-‘Askari, associated with the army and its base. Their house was deliberately placed within this military environment so that they could be watched. The location made surveillance easier and restricted the Imams’ ability to meet followers freely. The chapter therefore shows that political control operated not only through imprisonment and direct orders but also through the physical placement of the Imam’s residence. Geography itself became an instrument for monitoring and isolating the Imam.
questions.source_locator: Chapter 7: On the Topic of Imam al-Hassan al-‘Askari

questions.unit_title: Chapter 7: On the Topic of Imam al-Hassan al-‘Askari
questions.prompt: Develop Mutahhari’s comparison between the Abbasid surveillance of Imam al-‘Askari’s household and Pharaoh’s treatment of Bani Isra’il.
questions.answer: Mutahhari compares the Abbasid authorities’ fear of the promised Mahdi with Pharaoh’s fear of a foretold child from Bani Isra’il. In the account of Pharaoh, the ruler responded by killing newborn boys and appointing women to inspect households and identify pregnancies. Mutahhari says the caliphate system acted in a similar way toward Imam al-‘Askari: officials repeatedly searched his home because they feared that the promised Mahdi had been born, and women were sent to inspect the household after the Imam’s death. The comparison highlights a shared political pattern: a ruler who fears a future challenge attempts to prevent it by controlling births and surveilling families. The analogy expresses Mutahhari’s interpretation of the Abbasid motive and should not be treated as proof that every detail of the two historical accounts was identical.

questions.unit_title: Chapter 7: On the Topic of Imam al-Hassan al-‘Askari
questions.prompt: Describe the concealed birth of Imam al-Mahdi and the sequence of actions taken by the authorities to find him.
questions.answer: Mutahhari states that Imam al-Mahdi’s birth was concealed and known only to a limited group. During the child’s early years, Imam al-‘Askari introduced him to trusted Shi‘ah followers who came from different places, while the general public remained unaware. News nevertheless spread that a son had been born and was being hidden. The authorities periodically sent people to search the Imam’s house, especially around the time of his death, because they had heard that the child had already been born. After the Imam’s death, officers searched the house thoroughly and women were sent to inspect the women of the household for possible pregnancies. One slave girl was detained for a year because of a mistaken suspicion. Mutahhari says the child was six when his father died. The sequence shows both the regime’s anxiety and the limits of its surveillance: the searches did not give the authorities control over the succession described in the chapter.
questions.source_locator: Chapter 7: On the Topic of Imam al-Hassan al-‘Askari

questions.unit_title: Chapter 7: On the Topic of Imam al-Hassan al-‘Askari
questions.prompt: What does the detention of the suspected slave girl reveal about the reach and consequences of the authorities’ surveillance?
questions.answer: After Imam al-‘Askari’s death, officials did not limit their search to the Imam’s own person or to male members of the household. They sent women to inspect all the women in the home, including slave girls, to determine whether anyone might be pregnant. One slave girl was suspected and detained for an entire year before the authorities discovered that they had made a mistake. The episode demonstrates that the regime’s fear of the promised child extended surveillance into the private lives and bodies of women in the household. It also shows the human cost of acting on suspicion: a person could lose a year of freedom even though the suspicion was false. Mutahhari uses the episode to illustrate the extraordinary lengths to which the authorities went in trying to prevent the expected succession.
questions.source_locator: Chapter 7: On the Topic of Imam al-Hassan al-‘Askari

questions.unit_title: Chapter 7: On the Topic of Imam al-Hassan al-‘Askari
questions.prompt: Explain the significance of Hudayth’s title Jaddah and her role as a learned refuge for the Shi‘ah community.
questions.answer: Hudayth, the mother of Imam al-‘Askari, became known as Jaddah, or “grandmother,” because of her relationship to the Imam of the Time. Mutahhari emphasizes that her status was not merely inherited from her grandchild. She had her own dignity, learning, and special personality. Citing Muhaddith Qummi’s Al-Anwar al-Bahiyyah, he describes her as a shelter for the Shi‘ah after Imam al-‘Askari’s death. Followers brought their religious and doctrinal questions to her when they needed guidance. Her role was therefore both personal and communal: she was a respected scholar and a practical refuge for a community living under pressure and without ordinary public access to the hidden Imam. Mutahhari’s account presents her as an important link in the continuity of guidance during the transition to occultation.

questions.unit_title: Chapter 7: On the Topic of Imam al-Hassan al-‘Askari
questions.prompt: Explain Hakimah Khatun’s analogy between Imam al-‘Askari’s arrangement and Imam al-Husayn’s reliance on Lady Zaynab. What distinction does the analogy establish?
questions.answer: Hakimah Khatun explains that the hidden son of Imam al-‘Askari remained the true Imam, while Jaddah was the person whom followers should consult for practical problems. To explain how this could be, she refers to Imam al-Husayn: his true successor and inward trustee was Imam Zayn al-‘Abidin, yet he entrusted much of the outward and visible responsibility to his sister Zaynab. Hakimah says Imam al-‘Askari acted similarly. His inward trustee was his hidden son, but because he could not publicly identify the child as his successor, he outwardly entrusted the community’s practical affairs to Jaddah. The analogy distinguishes actual religious succession from the visible person who carries out practical responsibilities under dangerous circumstances. It does not mean that Jaddah replaced the Imam; rather, she served as the public point of reference while the hidden Imam remained the true authority.
questions.source_locator: Chapter 7: On the Topic of Imam al-Hassan al-‘Askari

questions.unit_title: Chapter 7: On the Topic of Imam al-Hassan al-‘Askari
questions.prompt: How does Mutahhari show that Imam al-‘Askari’s influence and authority were not dependent on freedom of movement or political power?
questions.answer: Mutahhari describes Imam al-‘Askari as living under severe restrictions: he was compelled to reside in a military quarter, closely watched, imprisoned at times, and prevented from meeting people freely. Yet the chapter also emphasizes his dignity and the respect he commanded. Visitors were affected by his bearing before he spoke, and even enemies and officials who pursued him could not resist showing him respect. His authority therefore did not arise from holding government office or controlling coercive power. It was expressed through his character, spiritual standing, and the reverence he inspired. The account contrasts the state’s physical control over the Imam’s movements with its inability to erase his moral influence. Mutahhari uses this contrast to show that spiritual authority can remain powerful even under political confinement.
questions.source_locator: Chapter 7: On the Topic of Imam al-Hassan al-‘Askari

questions.unit_title: Chapter 7: On the Topic of Imam al-Hassan al-‘Askari
questions.prompt: What is the central lesson of Chapter 7 about the continuity of religious guidance under surveillance and occultation?
questions.answer: The chapter portrays Imam al-‘Askari’s final years as a period of intense political surveillance because the authorities feared the birth of the promised Mahdi from his line. The Imam was confined and isolated, his home was repeatedly searched, and the household’s women were subjected to intrusive inspections. Nevertheless, Mutahhari describes the birth as concealed from the general public while trusted followers were informed, and he states that the child was six when his father died. After the Imam’s death, Jaddah served as a learned refuge for the Shi‘ah, while Hakimah Khatun affirmed that the hidden child remained the true Imam. The analogy with Imam al-Husayn and Lady Zaynab explains how a visible trustee could manage practical affairs without replacing the true successor. The chapter’s central lesson is that political surveillance could restrict public contact but could not, within the author’s theological framework, extinguish the continuity of Imamate and religious guidance.
